name: Lateral canthoplasty
lead: Lateral canthoplasty is eyelid surgery that repositions or tightens the lateral canthus, the outer corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet. In ophthalmic and plastic surgery it is used mainly to support or tighten a lax lower eyelid, to prevent or correct lid malposition after lower blepharoplasty, and in facial palsy and ectropion repair.[1][3][6][11]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed for a different aim: raising the outer corner to produce a more positive canthal tilt, a more almond or 'hunter' eye shape, or more visible sclera. Published surgical literature describes canthal procedures as supportive or functional, and no published study found here evaluates canthoplasty specifically for increasing canthal tilt in people with normal eyelid tone.[1][6]

Surgeons distinguish canthoplasty, which involves cutting and reattaching the lateral canthal tendon, from the more conservative canthopexy, which supports the lid with sutures without detaching the tendon. Reviews note that small adjustments in this area can produce large changes in lower eyelid shape, and that excessive tightening or midface elevation can lead to round-eye deformity or ectropion.[1][2]

paras: The canthus is the corner of the eye; the outer one is the lateral canthus. Wikipedia defines canthoplasty as plastic surgery on the medial canthus, the lateral canthus or both, and distinguishes it from canthotomy, which cuts the canthus to relieve orbital pressure.[10]

A review of aesthetic canthal suspension describes the options as canthopexy, an orbicularis sling and modified canthoplasty. Canthopexy is the most conservative; canthoplasty is generally reserved for more marked laxity, which is less common in people seeking cosmetic blepharoplasty.[1] A second review covers open and closed canthal suspension, commissure-sparing open canthoplasty and canthopexy, along with preoperative evaluation, recovery and complications.[6]

Canthal procedures are used for involutional lower lid laxity and ectropion, and a randomised trial has examined lateral tarsal strip surgery for epiphora in involutional ectropion.[8] In a prospective trial of 40 patients with paralytic lagophthalmos, lower lid lateral canthoplasty was performed in 14 patients who also had lid laxity alongside upper-lid gold weight implants.[7]

In aesthetic surgery, canthal support is advocated as a routine part of lower blepharoplasty to reduce the risk of lid malposition; a 10-year review of one surgeon's lower blepharoplasty practice with routine lateral canthal support is among the larger reports.[4] Reviews also describe canthal support in the setting of prominent globes or a negative vector, in which the cheek sits behind the eye.[1] Surgeons caution that a limited amount of midface lift is safe before round-eye deformity and ectropion result.[2]

Reviews of canthal suspension discuss complications including lid malposition, asymmetry and altered eyelid shape, because the area is delicate and small changes have large effects.[1][6] Post-blepharoplasty lower eyelid retraction is described as difficult to treat and as a point of failure when canthoplasty is under tension.[5]
Forum threads titled around canthoplasty 'botch rate' reflect community concern about outcomes.[13]

The published human literature on lateral canthoplasty concerns eyelid function and lower blepharoplasty support, including reviews, surgeon case series and small trials.[1][3][4][7][8] No study located examines lateral canthoplasty as a cosmetic procedure to change canthal tilt in people with normal eyelid tone.

On looksmax.org, members ask whether canthoplasty or canthopexy is better for improving sclera show or canthal tilt, and debate whether canthoplasty is appropriate for people under 40.[12][14][15] One thread poster describes eyes that look negatively tilted and droopy and asks what can be done, and a reply calls the procedure risky.[14]

Do-it-yourself canthoplasty has also become a topic, with at least one thread asking why the trend arose.[16] The wiki does not describe self-performed surgery; no research or surgical guideline recommends it.

lore.intro: The procedure is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a way to alter canthal tilt, with recurring disagreement over canthoplasty versus canthopexy and over age suitability.[12][14][15]

claims.claim: Canthoplasty can raise the outer eye corner for a more positive canthal tilt.
claims.believers: Members ask which procedure would change tilt or sclera show and some say canthopexy with fat grafts is preferable.[12]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews describe canthal procedures as supporting or tightening the lower lid; no study found tests canthoplasty for increasing canthal tilt cosmetically.[1][6]

claims.claim: Canthopexy is the better choice than canthoplasty for people under 40.
claims.believers: A thread title argues that those under 40 should choose canthopexy and some members repeat that canthoplasty is for people 30 and older.[15][11]
claims.experts: Reviews state canthopexy is the most conservative option and canthoplasty is reserved for marked laxity, which is less common in younger aesthetic patients.[1]

claims.claim: Canthoplasty carries a meaningful risk of botching the eye.
claims.believers: Members start threads on botch rate and one replier calls it risky and advises trying other options first.[13][14]
claims.experts: Reviews note that small adjustments around the canthus can alter lower eyelid shape substantially and that malposition is a known risk.[1][2]

claims.claim: Canthoplasty can be done at home.
claims.believers: Multiple threads about 'DIY canthoplasty' exist, with one asking why it became a trend.[16]
claims.experts: No published studies or surgical guidelines describe or support self-performed canthal surgery; the literature describes it as delicate surgery performed by trained surgeons.[1][6]

card.summary: Surgery on the outer eye corner, used medically for lid laxity and increasingly sought to raise canthal tilt; no studies test it for that cosmetic aim.
card.note: Cosmetic tilt change is untested; lid malposition risk is documented and DIY versions circulate online.

quick.overview:
Lateral canthoplasty reshapes or tightens the outer corner of the eye by working on the lateral canthal tendon. Surgeons use it to support a loose lower eyelid, for ectropion, and alongside lower blepharoplasty.

In looksmaxxing forums people ask about it for a more positive canthal tilt or a more almond eye. The published literature covers lid support, not cosmetic tilt, and forum users debate canthoplasty versus the gentler canthopexy.
quick.mechanism: The lateral canthal tendon is repositioned or tightened and anchored to the orbital rim, lifting and supporting the outer lid. Canthopexy uses sutures without detaching the tendon.
quick.risks: Reviews note that small changes can substantially alter lower eyelid shape and that malposition, round-eye deformity and ectropion are risks. Cosmetic canthal-tilt outcomes have not been studied, and self-performed versions discussed online have no published support.
